The Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbi Shmuel ben Uri Shraga Feivush, Author of "Beit Shmuel"
The Historical Period and the Background to the Splendor of His Work
In the second half of the seventeenth century the world of Torah in Europe underwent deep upheavals that changed the face of learning and halakhic ruling for generations [cite: 1, 2]. The period after the decrees of Tach and Tat (5408 and 5409) was characterized by a broad migration of Torah scholars from the centers of Torah in Poland westward, toward the German-speaking communities of Ashkenaz [cite: 1, 2]. This migration produced a fruitful encounter between the Polish method of study, whose distinctive mark was sharp pilpul and deep analysis of Talmudic topics, and the Ashkenazi tradition, which strove for order, for a defined custom and for practical decision [cite: 1, 2].
At that time the literature of commentaries on Rabbi Yosef Karo's "Shulchan Arukh" and the glosses of the Rema was in the midst of a flowering [cite: 1, 3]. While comprehensive and systematic commentaries had already been written on the sections "Orach Chaim" and "Yoreh De'ah" in the first half of the century, the section "Even HaEzer" – which deals with the laws of marriage, betrothal, divorce and abandoned wives (agunot) – remained relatively neglected in the world of Torah literature [cite: 1]. The severe legal complexity of these laws, together with the heavy halakhic responsibility involved in permitting a married woman to remarry, kept many decisors away from systematically writing a comprehensive work on the order of the Shulchan Arukh in this section [cite: 1]. Against this background arose the figure of Rabbi Shmuel ben Uri Shraga Feivush, who produced a fundamental and systematic commentary that became one of the most central and indispensable of the Shulchan Arukh's commentators [cite: 1, 2, 4].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Life, His Teachers and the Course of His Rabbinic Leadership
Rabbi Shmuel, son of Rabbi Uri Shraga Feivush, was born in the middle of the seventeenth century in the city of Wodzislaw (Waidislav) in Poland [cite: 1, 2, 5]. In his youth he was sent to study in the cradle of Polish Jewish scholarship – the yeshiva of Kraków (Krakow) – where he acquired most of his course of study from two of the great men of the generation [cite: 1, 2]. His first teacher was Rabbi Yehoshua Heshel ben Rabbi Yaakov, known as "Rabbi R. Heshil," one of the most prominent spiritual leaders of the generation [cite: 1, 2]. After the death of Rabbi R. Heshil, Rabbi Shmuel continued his course of studies with his successor in the rabbinate and in heading the yeshiva of Kraków, Rabbi Aryeh Leib ben Rabbi Zechariah Mendel, called Rabbi Aryeh Leib "the Long" [cite: 1, 2, 5].
Rabbi Aryeh Leib recognized the exalted abilities of his student and took him as a son-in-law for his daughter [cite: 1, 2]. This marriage joined Rabbi Shmuel to one of the most distinguished and influential families in the rabbinic world of his day, since his brothers-in-law were famous Torah scholars, among them Rabbi Yechezkiah Yehoshua Feivel Teomim, author of the book "Panim Meirot," and Rabbi Shaul ben Rabbi Heshil of Kraków [cite: 1, 2]. After his marriage Rabbi Shmuel began to hold Torah offices; some sources note that he served as a preacher and "maggid meisharim" in Lvov, although some doubt this fact [cite: 2]. He was later appointed Av Beit Din and mara de-atra in the community of Szydłów in Poland, where he served in the rabbinate and where he began writing his great work [cite: 2, 4].
In the year 5451 (1691) an approach reached him from the committee of the community of Fürth in Germany – one of the important and central communities in Ashkenaz – to take upon himself the spiritual leadership of the city [cite: 2]. Rabbi Shmuel accepted the offer and arrived in Fürth in the winter of 5452 (1692), where he served as Av Beit Din, mara de-atra and head of the local yeshiva for about three years [cite: 2]. In the year 5454 (1694) Rabbi Shmuel left Fürth and returned to Poland, to his former post in Szydłów [cite: 2]. Researchers and early sources raise various conjectures about his sudden departure from Ashkenaz, attributing it to his longing for his native land and for the Polish method of study, or alternatively to internal disputes that had arisen at that time in the community of Fürth [cite: 2]. Rabbi Shmuel led the community of Szydłów until the day of his death and was buried in the city's cemetery [cite: 2]. The date of his death is not definite in the sources, but it is agreed that he died in the first years of the 18th century, most likely between the years 5459 (1699) and 5467 (1706) [cite: 1, 2].

First rabbinate | Szydłów (Poland) [cite: 2, 4] | The 80s of the 17th century [cite: 4] | Composition of the first edition of the book "Beit Shmuel" [cite: 2, 4].

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Book "Beit Shmuel": The Scope of the Work, the Process of Its Formation and the Printing of "Apei Ravrevei"
When he came to write his book on the section Even HaEzer, Rabbi Shmuel referred explicitly to the state of neglect of study in this section of the Shulchan Arukh, and, regarding his study of it, recommended the verse "The stone which the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone" [cite: 1]. By a linguistic allusion to the word "Even" ("stone") – the first letters of "Even HaEzer" – Rabbi Shmuel sought to turn the halakhic section that had been shunned in the eyes of many students into the focus of theoretical and halakhic engagement [cite: 1]. The work is built with great concision, presenting the sources of the law, clarifying the views of the Rishonim and Acharonim, and giving a clear and reasoned decision on the tangled topics of the laws of marriage and divorce [cite: 1, 5, 6].
The book "Beit Shmuel" underwent a process of development and halakhic refinement and was published in two main editions during the author's lifetime [cite: 4, 7]. The first edition (mahadura kamma) was printed in 5449 (1689) in the city of Dyhernfurth, at the press of Shabtai Meshorer Bass [cite: 4, 5]. This edition included the running commentary alongside fundamental appendices: "Kuntres Agunot," which gathers in brief the responses of the decisors on section 17, the "Seder HaGet" of Rabbi Yaakov Margalit, and the "Seder Gittin" of Rabbi Yechiel Michel of Kraków, with detailed additions and glosses from the study hall of Rabbi Shmuel [cite: 5]. After his move to Fürth, the author devoted himself to a renewed and expanded revision of his work [cite: 2, 4]. The second edition (mahadura batra) was printed in Fürth in 5454 (1694), in which he corrected objections, added many sources and deepened his analyses [cite: 2, 4]. Our master Rabbi Chaim Yosef David Azulai (the Chida) laid down in his book "Shem HaGedolim" a decisive bibliographical-halakhic rule, according to which no heed is to be paid to the first edition of the book "Beit Shmuel" where it differs from the later edition, since the author himself retracted and corrected his conclusions [cite: 7].
Parameter of Comparison | First Edition (Dyhernfurth, 5449) | Later Edition (Fürth, 5454)
Year and Place of Printing | 1689 (5449), Dyhernfurth [cite: 4, 5] | 1694 (5454), Fürth [cite: 2, 4]
Printing House | The press of Shabtai Meshorer Bass of Prague [cite: 5] | The Fürth press [cite: 2, 4]
Contents of the Appendices | Kuntres Agunot, Seder HaGet and Seder Gittin [cite: 5] | A revised, corrected and expanded text within the body of the commentary [cite: 4, 7]
Halakhic Standing for Later Generations | Set aside in favor of the later Fürth edition [cite: 7] | The canonical edition, printed in all editions of the Shulchan Arukh [cite: 4, 7]
In parallel with Rabbi Shmuel's work, another great decisor in Poland – Rabbi Moshe Lima, Av Beit Din of Vilna – composed a fundamental commentary on the section Even HaEzer called "Chelkat Mechokek" [cite: 1, 3, 5]. The printers of the Shulchan Arukh recognized the superiority of the two works and decided to set them side by side, on the two sides of the text of the Shulchan Arukh and the Rema [cite: 1, 3, 4]. The joint edition that included "Chelkat Mechokek" and "Beit Shmuel" received the collective name "Apei Ravrevei," based on the Aramaic translation of the phrase "Panim Gedolot" ("great faces"), and from then until today the two works are printed together in most editions of the Shulchan Arukh [cite: 1, 2, 3].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Halakhic Method, His Manner of Study and Analysis of Topics
Rabbi Shmuel's halakhic method in the commentary "Beit Shmuel" distinctly combines deep Polish yeshiva analysis with the demand for practical and clear ruling [cite: 1, 2]. His manner of study is characterized by a fundamental analysis of the legal and halakhic concepts underlying the topics [cite: 6, 8]. Thus, for example, in his discussions of a man who betroths a woman against her will, Rabbi Shmuel examines the halakhic mechanism of "talya ve-zabin" (a sale made under compulsion) and explains why in forced betrothals of a woman the betrothal does not take effect [cite: 6]. He clarifies that although by biological and legal law the betrothal should have taken effect, the Sages annulled it from him ("afka'inhu rabbanan le-kiddushin minei") because he acted improperly [cite: 6]. Following this, he compares compulsion of the woman with compulsion of the man: whereas a man who coerces a woman is not betrothed, owing to a rabbinic enactment, a man who was coerced to betroth – his betrothal is a valid betrothal, since it is in his power to divorce her against her will [cite: 6]. This analysis leads him to examine the halakhic implications in our time, after the enactment of Rabbenu Gershom forbidding divorcing a woman against her will, as he examines whether the status of a man who was coerced to betroth has changed, or whether coercion in betrothal was excluded from this enactment [cite: 6].
Another distinctive feature of Rabbi Shmuel's approach is the constant confrontation and careful clarification between the differing views of the early decisors – such as the Rambam, the Ra'avad, the Ramban, the Rashba, the Rif and the Ran – and the rulings of the later authorities who preceded him, among them the Taz, the Shach, the Sma and the "Chelkat Mechokek" [cite: 5, 6, 8]. In the laws of a single witness in betrothal and situations of contradiction between witnesses, Rabbi Shmuel analyzes the weight of the "presumption of being unmarried" and its definitions in situations of "two against two" or a single witness who denies a woman's betrothal [cite: 8]. He presents the dispute between the Rambam and the other Rishonim in the case where one witness says "she was betrothed" and another witness contradicts him, and he is precise about the wording of the Shulchan Arukh and the Rema in order to reconcile complex contradictions between different sections of the book [cite: 6, 8].
Beyond the theoretical depth, the style of the "Beit Shmuel" is distinguished by concision and a rare capacity for compression [cite: 1, 6]. In a few lines Rabbi Shmuel manages to summarize difficult Talmudic topics, lay out the views of the Rishonim, and decide the halakha in practice in a clear and sharp manner [cite: 1, 6]. This concentrated style made the work a central working tool for judges and halakhic instructors who need well-founded decisions on topics of Even HaEzer [cite: 1, 2].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Additional Works, Family, Students and Legacy for Generations
Although Rabbi Shmuel's name is forever linked to his commentary on Even HaEzer, the scope of his Torah creation went beyond the bounds of this work [cite: 2]. Historical sources and family testimonies indicate that Rabbi Shmuel also composed a comprehensive commentary on the section "Yoreh De'ah" of the Shulchan Arukh [cite: 2]. His son-in-law, Rabbi Uri Feivush Hamburger, describes in his introduction to the book "Urim VeTumim" the greatness of his father-in-law's stature and expresses a prayer that he may merit to publish his writings on Yoreh De'ah [cite: 2]. Sadly, these writings did not merit to see print and have not reached us [cite: 2]. In addition, from his tenure as head of a yeshiva and as Av Beit Din in Szydłów and Fürth, Rabbi Shmuel composed responsa on halakha and homilies, some of which were embedded in the books of the sages of his generation [cite: 2, 5].
Rabbi Shmuel raised a splendid dynasty of Torah scholars and rabbinic leaders who influenced European Jewry [cite: 2]. His son, Rabbi Yosef, was the father of Rabbi Shmuel who served as Av Beit Din of Amdur and Manisk (Minsk), and his other sons were Rabbi Aryeh Leib and Rabbi Shilem [cite: 2]. Among his sons-in-law stood out Rabbi Uri Feivush Hamburger, who later moved to London and served as the first chief rabbi of the Ashkenazi community in Britain, Rabbi Betzalel Slutzki, and Rabbi Yitzchak Isaac of Amdur [cite: 2]. Rabbi Shmuel's family ties linked him to the most distinguished rabbinic dynasties in Eastern Europe, among them the families Teomim and Ornstein and the descendants of Rabbi Shaul Wahl [cite: 2].
During his tenure as head of a yeshiva in Fürth and in Szydłów, Rabbi Shmuel raised many students who served in the rabbinate throughout Ashkenaz and Poland [cite: 2]. The yeshiva of Fürth under his leadership was considered one of the most attractive Torah centers in Germany [cite: 2]. However, Rabbi Shmuel's main and lasting influence is in his written legacy [cite: 1, 2, 3]. From the day of the printing of his second edition of "Beit Shmuel" within "Apei Ravrevei," the book became the cornerstone of halakhic ruling in the section Even HaEzer [cite: 1, 3, 4]. The greatest decisors of the following centuries – among them Rabbi Yechezkel Landau, author of the "Noda bi-Yehuda," Rabbi Moshe Sofer, author of the "Chatam Sofer," the authors of the "Pitchei Teshuva" and the "Arukh HaShulchan," and up to the judges of the rabbinical courts in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries – regard the commentary "Beit Shmuel" as a primary source and a binding starting point in every halakhic discussion of the laws of marriage, divorce and abandoned wives [cite: 1, 2, 3].
